newsitem.title: Italy: Italian government wins latest confidence test.
newsitem.headline: Italian government wins latest confidence test.

text.p: Italy's centre-left government won a confidence vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) on Thursday which it had called to push through a draft law on reforms of the civil service and public administration.
The victory by 315 votes to 185 ensured passage of articles of the bill which had not yet been debated because of what the government argued were opposition delaying tactics.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi relies for his majority in the lower house on the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which almost brought down the government last week by voting against deployment of Italian troops in Albania.
It backed the government in confidence tests in both houses of parliament called last week over the Albania rift and again supported Prodi on Thursday.
The draft bill is designed to simplify Italy's stifling public bureaucracy and transfer many of the powers now held by national civil servants to local and regional authorities.
It passed through the Senate (upper house) last July but had been held up in the lower house by opposition politicians absenting themselves from the chamber and denying a quorum.
A vote on the bill itself is scheduled for April 29 after which it must return to the Senate for another reading.

Many deputies from the conservative opposition party Forza Italia boycotted Thursday's vote in protest at what they argued was arrogance in the way the confidence test was called by the bill's sponsor, Regional Affairs Minister Franco Bassanini.
Governments have traditionally resorted to confidence votes to push through legislation in the face of filibustering and because of the snail's pace of parliamentary work in Italy.

Prodi's government has also been forced to use the tactic to avoid a legislative vacuum after a Constitutional Court ruling last year that cabinet decrees, a favoured form of law-making, could not be re-issued when they expire after 60 days.
The opposition interpreted the latest vote as a sign of weakness by Prodi's coalition government, installed last May after a general election victory one year ago on Sunday.
"There is a tradition in Italian parliamentary history. The weaker the government, the more it resorts to confidence votes," said Gianfranco Fini, leader of the hard-right National Alliance.
"The Prodi government in 11 months, if I remember correctly, is on its 13th or 14th request for a confidence vote. That shows that it is politically very weak," he said.
